Motivation

The global transition towards sustainable energy and transportation has seen a rapid increase in the adoption of Electric Vehicles (EV). While this shift brings forth many environmental and economic benefits, it also presents new challenges for the power systems. As EVs have a high energy consumption when charging, several studies have predicted the consequences of the rapid integration of EVs. One of these studies [2] analyses how the increase in EVs has strained local distributional grids in Norway. The study found that EVs have increased the total energy electricity use in Norway by 0.42% in 2020. Statnett also states that the electric energy use for transportation will be 20 TWh by 2030 in Norway [3]. From this, it is evident that the transportation sector is going to make a substantial impact on the grid.

text: Objective/Contributions

This thesis aims to evaluate the costs and potential benefits of a flexible EVPL connected to an office building participating in an IBDRP. These programs offer incentives for modifying consumption patterns. This study focuses on optimizing EV charging and minimizing the associated costs, and examines how participation in the IBDRP affects operational performance and costs. Additionally, the thesis explores Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology to analyze how the technology affects operational performance, with and without IBDR-participation. The IBDRP allows participation with varying notice times before activation, impacting operational decisions due to the uncertain activation notification. To the author's knowledge, limited work has looked into IBDR programs with different notice times. In this thesis this is addressed by integrating notice time into scheduling decisions within the Receding Horizon (RH)-framework to react to the flexibility needs.

text: Electricity grid

An electricity grid is defined as a network where electricity is delivered from producers to consumers. The main elements in an electricity grid are power stations, electrical substations, transformers, transmission systems, and distribution systems [8]. In this section, the transmission- and distribution system is further explained.

text: Transmission System

The Transmission System Operator (TSO) is the administrative body that is responsible for building, managing, and maintaining the transmission grid [9]. The transmission grid connects producers with consumers in a nationwide system together with interconnections between other countries [10]. The transmission grid carries a high voltage, usually 300 to 420 kV, with certain parts of Norway having lines carrying 132 kV. Due to the cost of establishing and maintaining such a large infrastructure, a TSO is often a monopoly and therefore subject to strict regulations. In day-to-day operations, a TSO is responsible for maintaining a continuous balance between electricity supply from power stations and the demand from consumers, and also ensuring the provision of reserves that will allow for sudden contingencies [11]. The only TSO in Norway is Statnett, which is a state-owned company under the oil- and energy department.

text: Distribution System

The Distribution System Operator (DSO) is a key entity in the energy sector responsible for managing and operating the distribution system, which delivers electricity from the high-voltage transmission system to end-users. DSOs are responsible for the real-time operation of the distribution grid, ensuring the balance between electricity supply and demand. DSOs perform maintenance on the grid, including power lines, transformers, and substations. The service provided ensures a reliable power supply to end-users, by working to make the grid resilient against disruptions. In Norway, the distribution grid is divided into two levels [10]: The regional distribution grid, serves as the intermediary, connecting the transmission grid to the distribution grid. This grid can also include higher voltage production and consumption radials. The regional typically operates at a voltage of 33 to 132 kV. The local distribution grid supplied electricity to smaller end-users. This grid operates at voltages up to 22 kV and is split into high-voltage and low-voltage segments. The threshold between these segments is 1 kV, with the low voltage distribution to standard consumers normally carrying 400 V or 230 V.

section_title: Challenges in the Norwegian Power System
text: Increased renewable power production and the electrification of the transport sector are necessary to meet global emission goals but also bring forth many challenges for the grid operators. New larger renewable power production such as solar and wind is connected to the grid through converters [12]. This can worsen the grid stability, especially in Norway where the grid is built around hydropower-generation which is connected to the grid through synchronous generators. The synchronous generators are synchronized to the grid frequency while strengthening the frequency stability of the system. There is also an increase in distributed energy production, mostly through solar, which can cause local grid-stability issues [13]. The distributed energy production is more often located in weaker parts of the grid further out in the system, which is more prone to grid issues. Problems which were pointed out due to local solar production are voltage quality issues and thermal loads in cables and transformers.

Not having enough reserves can lead to market constraints, and in worst-case a forced disconnection of consumers or producers. text: The Norwegian Pricing Model
The power market

In Norway, all power trading is done through the European power exchange Nord Pool [14]. Nord Pool was founded in 1993 as Statnett Marked AS, as the Norwegian government deregulated the market for power trading. Throughout the years, Nord Pool has expanded further out in Europe, and now provides services in most of northern Europe. Nord Pool is an exchange built up from two main markets, namely the financial market and the physical market. Based on the scope of this thesis, only the physical is further discussed.

text: Figure 2.2.1: The Nord Pool Market [16]
The Day-Ahead Market

In the day-ahead market customers can sell or buy energy for the next 24 hours in a closed auction. Orders are matched to maximize social welfare while taking network constraints provided by transmission system operators into consideration [17]. This ensures that the power system is balanced before delivery [18]. Available capacities on interconnectors and in the grid are published at 10:00 CET (Central European Time). After this, the buyers and sellers have until 12:00 CET to submit their final bids to Nord Pool auction for delivery hours the next day. The market results are typically published before 13:00 CET and are referred to as spot prices [17]. Between the clearing of the spot price market and the delivery hour, the market participants can adjust their market position in the intra-day market [18].

text: Grid tariff

To cover the costs of grid operation, DSOs typically implement a grid tariff, which requires end-users to pay for the transportation of energy. The grid tariff usually consists of a volumetric cost based on the energy consumption, a fixed cost, and on commercial buildings there is a capacity-based cost which in this thesis is called the demand charge. Residential customers were introduced to the capacity-based grid tariff in 2022. The rates on the grid tariff and the contents are set by the respective DSOs. The Norwegian Energy Regulatory Authority (RME) overlooks the income from the grid tariffs and checks that the DSOs income does not surpass the regulated amount [4].

Demand response

A common initiative of DSM is Demand Response (DR). DR can be defined as the changes in electricity usage by end-use customers from their normal consumption patterns in response to changes in the price of electricity over time or grid reliability concerns [22] [23]. Demand Response Programs (DRP) can be used to reduce energy costs, reduce the variation in electricity prices, and make a more reliable power system. The DRPs performance can be measured by peak load reduction and demand elasticity [24]. It can be particularly challenging to create demand charge programs which fairly reflects the costs to the DSOs [25]. In Norway, a DRP was implemented for all household end-users in 2022 when a demand charge was implemented in the grid tariff, with the intention of making the customers aware of their peak power usage [26].

text: Price-based demand response

Price-Based Demand Response (PBDR) is a strategy that encourages consumers to adjust their electricity consumption patterns in response to price signals [27]. The purpose is to signal the customers to change their consumption to better reflect the grid situation. The customers are "punished" with higher electricity costs if the signal is ignored. A common way of introducing PBDR is by providing accurate spot price data. Before the introduction of smart meters in Norway, the spot price data was given as a monthly average. By 2019, all Norwegian homes had a digital smart-meter installed [28]. The recent introduction of smart meters in Norwegian households has made hourly power consumption data available for power and grid companies, and spot price data is now provided in an hourly resolution. Hourly spot prices make it possible for the end-users to adjust their demand more accurately to save costs and help reduce peaks in the grid.

text: 2.3.1.2 Incentive-based demand response

Incentive-based Demand Response (IBDR) provides fixed or time-varying incentives to participating customers for reducing their electricity usage [30]. IBDR works by sending signals to the end-users, notifying them to reduce their electricity consumption in periods when electricity demand is high or when there is a need to stabilize the grid. This might involve adjusting the heating, delaying the use of certain appliances, or adjusting the EV charging. IBDR being a voluntary agreement, consumer engagement and willingness to participate are important factors for IBDR being a successful strategy.

An example is Glitre Nett and their electricity tariff for large businesses and commercial customers with adequate power consumption [33]. Here a percentage-wise reduction in the DCC is offered for consumers, in which the size of the reduction is based on how preemptive the signal for the request must be sent.

text: EV charging

In this section, the goal is to map the categories of chargers in the market, and how they can facilitate EVs a flexible resource. An essential distinction among EV chargers lies in their classification as either passive or smart chargers. A passive charger is defined as a charger that supplies a constant power flow, without any consideration to the battery status [37]. A smart charger can consider the battery status, resulting in a dynamic power flow. A smart charger can also enable intelligent charging management when connected to the grid, using a communication module [37]. Enabling communication with the grid, a smart charger can charge an EV during off-peak hours. The integration of smart chargers can also contribute to the efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of the electric grid [37][38].

text: Mode 1 chargers refer to regular or slow charging from standard power outlets [39], and are defined as passive chargers. These chargers are the least safe chargers, as they are connected directly to the grid with no built-in safety functions. The use of this charger would only have a flexible potential by manually disconnecting the charger.

text: Bi-directional charging

A bi-directional charger is a charger with a dual-direction power flow, which means that the power can be transferred to and from the EV [41]. The vehicle-to-building (V2B) technology makes it possible for the EV to extract energy from a building, or transfer its energy to a building. Thus, V2B technologies can contribute to the development of smart buildings [42]. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) refers to the bi-directional power flow between EV and the power grid [43]. V2G technology can be used to feed power back into the power grid during peak hours, resulting in grid balancing and peak shaving.

section_title: Grid problems due to EV integration
text: A study from Canada considered the integration of EVs into the distribution grid, where the impacts of uncoordinated charging were evaluated on a real test feeder [51]. It was found that for normal and fast charging scenarios, the uncoordinated charging led to unacceptable voltage drops in remote buses, and the feeder line loading constraint was violated at 15% and 25% EV penetration for fast charging and normal charging respectively. Another case study was done on the power system on the Danish island of Bornholm [52], which analyzed the impacts of EV penetration on the grid. For the uncontrolled study, the feasible integration of EVs was 10%, while the controlled charging could handle the integration more effectively. Voltage drops are found to be the limiting factor, and the peak demand in the network is increased by 31% for a 50% EV integration controlled charging scenario. From the literature, it is evident that increased EV penetration with uncontrolled charging significantly increases peak demand and strains the grid. Having more flexible EV charging is one way to combat this.

text: Winschermann et al. studied the significance of historical data in enhancing EV charging strategies at office buildings [38]. Given the challenges posed by the high energy demands of EVs on the electrical grid, smart charging was proposed as a potential solution. In the study, historical data from an office parking lot, specifically focusing on arrival times, energy requirements, and dwell times, was used to determine how past data mirrors real-time operations. An algorithm was used to construct a power charging profile for EVs based on user-specific parameters. Using a greedy charging approach in office settings can result in high power peaks due to synchronized arrivals. Here, greedy charging entails charging without an energy management system, which charges at the maximum available power from the plug-in. Using historical data for efficient planning helped reduce the peaks by 50%. Complete historical data which concerned arrival and departure times and energy requirements, was found to be essential for efficient planning. text: A study conducted by Yee Ting Chai et al. [41] introduces a two-stage optimization method for EVs in a V2G program at an office building. For the V2G program to work, the scheme must address both the needs of EVs and building owners. For building owners, EVs need to be reliably present to supply power. EV owners, on the other hand, should benefit financially without V2G affecting their travel plans. To achieve this, the EV owners are allowed to reach their desired State of Charge (SOC) at any time by raising the energy anxiety factor. The proposed method uses day-ahead optimization based on expected loads and EV patterns, aiming to cut electricity costs. Then, in the second stage, a real-time optimization adjusts to actual EV behaviors. The simulations show promising results, although it is shown to be difficult to consider the monthly peak demand when optimizing for shorter intervals.

Findings from different studies vary on whether V2G has acceptable or detrimental impacts on battery degradation. text: Model Predictive Control Optimization

Model predictive control (MPC), also known as receding horizon control, moving horizon control, or rolling horizon control, is a feedback control technique that solves an optimization problem at each time step to determine the optimal control actions over a fixed time horizon [71]. Normally MPC consists of three stages; a model to predict future outputs, calculate control actions to optimize performance, and apply a horizon strategy to dynamically update new information in the optimization process when new information becomes available [72]. MPC is a well used feedback control technique and has been used since 1980 [71]. MPC algorithms often solve problems under uncertainty or large-scale optimization problems [73], and are often used to solve MSSP problems [74]. MPC algorithms have among other things become important in the operation of energy systems because the optimal operation must account for the uncertainty of consumer's behavior, weather conditions, and power generation from renewable energy sources [75]. Model Description

This chapter introduces the model that was created to minimize the electricity costs for an office building with an EVPL. The model setup and methodology are presented in detail, covering the motivations and assumptions for the choices made.

text: Model overview

The modeling of the operation of the office building with a connected EVPL requires detailed information on a short-term basis to make hourly operational decisions. The system is also modeled over one month to consider the monthly grid tariff costs. The system is investigated for participation in an IBDRP and is also subject to day-ahead spot prices, which require dynamic updates of information. A version of a RH-framework is introduced which introduces dynamic horizons that dynamically update the information available in the optimization problem. The information available to the EVPL is on a daily basis, making it beneficial to decompose the monthly problem into daily stages. The monthly peak is the only state variable of the model, and information about the monthly peak is carried over between the daily stages.

Case Study

The primary goal of this study is to investigate how the operation of a flexible EVPL can reduce cost of operation and peak consumption for an office building while offering grid services. To do this, a case study is developed to investigate how the different technologies and IBDRP signals influence the decisions and the resulting strategies. This chapter gives an introduction to the cases and scenarios, together with an analysis of the input data and the parameters used in the optimizing frameworks.

It is assumed that the EVPL is approved for offering flexibility to the local DSO as part of an IBDRP. The IBDRP is based on the flexible consumption IBDRP from the DSO Glitre Nett [6], which includes different product classes based on the notice time prior to activation. The objective of this tariff is to provide grid stability services by reducing the EVPL demand when the DSO requests. By participating in this program, the office building receives economic incentives as a percentage reduction on the DCC. The incentive offers higher rewards for shorter notice times, as presented in Table 6.2.4.

Stochastic office building data

The stochasticity of the model is based on the uncertain office-building load. Only the SDDP-framework considers the stochastic data. Three scenarios are assumed for each decision stage, low, medium, and high. The medium scenario is equal to the historical office load data, presented in Section 6.2.1. High and low scenarios have a 30 % higher and lower office building demand respectively. The motivation behind the stochastic scenarios is to have a more realistic model with an uncertain future. The scenario percentages and probabilities for high and low scenarios are chosen quite arbitrarily and are not based on any previous work. The transition probabilities between each scenario are only based on which scenario is next. In other words, the origin scenario that is being transitioned from does not affect the transition probability. The probability of the medium scenario is 50%, high is 25%, and low is 25%. The cuts that are exported to be used in the short-term planning in RH are the medium scenario cuts. In some cases, deterministic cuts are used. These cuts are in practice generated by making the high and low scenarios equal to the medium scenario.

text: Prediction horizons

The RH-framework uses the historical measured data for the office building load, which is equivalent to only using the medium scenarios. Thus, the RH-framework uses deterministic data which does not include any uncertainties. In the RH-framework, the length of the three horizons has to be determined. The SH considers the overall operational period of one month. The CH represents the hour of operation that is to be determined, resulting in a horizon of one hour. Lastly, the PH has a horizon equal to the time remaining of the operating day, thus the horizon will continuously decrease until the spot prices for the next day are revealed. The RH-framework has a new PH for each time step, where every PH receives a simplified representation of the rest of the SH from the linear cuts provided by the SDDP-framework. In Norway, the spot prices for the next day are revealed at 1 PM [96], thus at 1 PM, the RH-framework will receive the spot prices for the next day. When this happens, the PH is expanded from 12 to 36 hours, revealing information about the next day of operation. When the new information is revealed, the PH will also receive new linear cuts from the SDDP-framework, which now presents a simplified representation of the cost of the remaining SH. The dynamic updating of the RH horizons is presented in 6.3.1, where the blue future cost curve is replaced with the red future cost curve considering the next day of operation.

Model Cases

The goal of Case 0 (C0) is to analyze the impact of the future cost curves provided by the SDDP-framework, and also establish an analysis that represents the system when no IBDR-signal is given. C0 will consider two months, namely the winter month March, and the summer month September. Three further case studies are developed, which are analyzed for for the month of March, each with its own goal and motivation. The common goal of the three cases is to analyze the consequences of IBDR-signals under different scenarios. Case 1 (C1) and Case 2 (C2) both analyze the consequences of IBDR-signals when no economic incentives are given to the office building, and rather look at the operational impact of the requested IBDR activations. In C2, V2G technology is implemented to facilitate a throttling signal that is greater than the maximum power capacity of the EVPL. Lastly, Case 3 (C3) includes economic incentives to see if an IBDRP can be of economic gain for the office building operator.

text: SDDPs quality of only optimizing for the interesting state variable values is easily observed in the plots. In Figure 7.1.2b the marginal cost is seen to be constant at a lower value than the DCC for peak values above 260 kWh/h. This is an inaccuracy caused by the model never optimizing for peaks this high. The same phenomena can be seen for peak values lower than 215 kWh/h. Here, days 13 and later have a marginal cost higher than zero, which would not have been the case in reality. These days are not optimized and tested on these low peak values, and these values therefore lack detailed information on the cost of raising the peaks. The increased detail and accuracy in the peaks of interest decrease the detail and accuracy in the peaks outside of the researched range. Outer-lying peaks are represented poorly as they are not tested at all of the possible peak values. This could cause problems if something out of the ordinary (such as an IBDRP throttling signal) shifts the peak values outside of the researched range. Using a decomposition method that discretizes the state variable range into regular intervals such as SDP would increase the future-cost prediction accuracy for outer-lying peaks, but would also lead to inaccuracies between the discrete states used.

text: As previously mentioned, the SDDP-framework does not consider the IBDR-signals, thus the future cost curves struggle to give the RH-framework an accurate estimation if the peak is raised too high by the IBDR-signals. When the PH in the RH-framework receives the IBDR-signal, it has to make a new plan for how to cover the load which was previously planned in the throttling hour. On day 6, when the IBDR-signal is given, the PH plans to solve the reduced EV charging capacity in the activation hour by being mostly proactive, shifting energy to before the throttle hour, which results in a monthly peak increase. The RH-framework does not know that the IBDR-signal will also occur the next day, which also results in a peak increase. The figure shows how the system is one day behind in raising the peak. If this new monthly peak was known for day 6, the system could potentially utilize this to have more flexibility regarding the spot prices.

The goal of this section is to analyze the economical impact of the IBDRP for the the worst-case scenario. This analysis is presented in Table 7.2.2. text: The marginal cost increases significantly for both a notice time of 2 and 0 hours. There is a clear breaking point at around 60 kW reduced EV charging capacity, where the system can no longer avoid increasing the peak, as seen in Figure 7.2.6b, and the subsequent demand charge. The 2 hour notice time case quickly plateaus at a level around 15 NOK/kW, which suggests that the model has more than one hour to assign charging to. From Figure 7.2.6b, the peak can be seen to steadily rise 10 kWh/h in the interval when the reduced EV charging ranges from 60 to 90 kW, which results in a rate of increase on the peak value of around 0,33 kW per kW recused EV capacity. Including the DCC, this would result in a marginal cost of increasing the peak equal to 57.16/3 = 19.05 NOK/kW. The difference between this marginal cost and the marginal cost seen in the plot at around 15 NOK/kW is the profit from increased flexibility to take advantage of spot price variation in the rest of the month. The 0 hour notice time only has one hour to allocate the peak-increase to, observed with marginal cost being close to the DCC. This indicates that two of the three hours used to distribute the peak increase in the 2 hour notice time case are before the notice time signal, which the 0 hour notice time case does not have "access" to when handling the IBDR-signal.

However, there is only one day in the month with ENS, as this is the only day which maximizes maximizes the EV charging capacity in the hours after the activation. If this critical day does not receive an IBDR-signal, it can be expected that a larger EV capacity reduction can be applied in the activation hour without resulting in ENS. However, it is found that when the EV capacity is reduced by 5 kW, there is ENS for days 7, 18, 28, and 31. There is shown to be limited flexibility in the system for a notice time of 0 hours as it struggles to avoid ENS. At the same time, it is seen from Figure 7.4.4 that if an IBDR-signal is not given on day 7, the peak does not increase, resulting in a changed planned EV charging. This entails that it is difficult to deduce which days of the month which are critical for the operation to avoid ENS.

text: Conclusion
Conclusion

This thesis investigated how an electric vehicle parking lot (EVPL) can use flexible resources to reduce the cost of operation for an office building while providing grid stability services through an incentive-based demand response program (IBDRP). In the thesis a model is developed using the decomposition method Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming (SDDP) and the real-time operation framework of Receding Horizon (RH). The SDDP-framework creates future cost curves which represent the future cost of increasing the peak demand. The future cost curves are seen to be accurate in the normal operating interval for the peak values, but can encounter inaccuracies in the outer-lying peak values. The RH-framework is implemented so that the operation of the EVPL can be optimized while simultaneously handling sudden IBDRP-signals.

In the worst-case scenario with maximum throttling at hour 12 every weekday, the 12 hour notice time is proven to handle the unexpected signal quite easily, with only a 0.57% cost increase compared to BC. It was shown through the sensitivity analysis that the marginal cost of providing grid services through an IBDR-signal was 0,047 NOK/kW at the highest, which would be a cheap source of flexibility for the DSO. However, the model struggles with limited flexibility for the shorter notice times, not being able to reallocate all of the displaced energy.

In this thesis, the real-time RH optimization framework used deterministic input data. It would be interesting to include a scenario picker into the model similar as to what was done in SDDP. A weighted forecast that predicts what hours is likely to have throttle activation could also be an interesting addition to the model. Implementing a different decomposition method than SDDP would also be interesting for comparison purposes.

text: When testing the model for different IBDRP-signals, only three notice times were considered, which were part of an already existing program. It would be interesting to perform a sensitivity analysis on which notice times the system can handle for different parameters. It would also be interesting to analyze the system for different activation hours. Also, the system investigated in this thesis was modeled as an aggregated load. It could be beneficial to try to model the system as a non aggregated EVPL. Although this would require a lot of data on each individual EV, the benefits could be a more realistic and detailed modeling.
